summary: Defines an alternative connection model for Message Session Relay Protocol endpoints using COMEDIA, letting endpoints behind NATs negotiate which side opens the TCP connection. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people behind locked doors each need to decide who knocks first. This helps chat programs agree on that so the connection works.

questions: how does msrp negotiate connection direction
subtitle: Let endpoints behind firewalls negotiate who initiates the connection.

tldr.problem: MSRP (Message Session Relay Protocol) normally requires the sender of the session offer to open the TCP connection. When one endpoint is behind a NAT, this fails because the NAT blocks incoming connections unless the endpoint initiated them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adopts COMEDIA (Connection-Oriented Media), an SDP mechanism that lets both sides negotiate which endpoint will open the connection. An endpoint behind a NAT can request to be the one opening the connection, allowing the TCP connection to pass through its NAT.
tldr.outcome: MSRP endpoints behind NATs can now communicate without relays or complex NAT traversal mechanisms, using standardized SDP attributes to agree on connection direction.

today: RFC 6135 is a Proposed Standard. Major messaging platforms using MSRP, including OMA (Open Mobile Alliance) Instant Messaging, rely on COMEDIA for NAT traversal in real-world deployments behind NATs. The RFC remains in effect and is widely supported by MSRP implementations.

sections.title: The NAT Problem with MSRP
sections.content:
MSRP is a protocol for relaying messages between endpoints in a media session. Normally, the endpoint that sends the SDP offer (the "offerer") becomes the active party and must open the TCP connection to the remote endpoint.

This works fine on the open Internet, but fails when an endpoint sits behind a Network Address Translator (NAT). A NAT blocks incoming TCP connections to protect the internal network. If the offerer is behind a NAT and must open a connection to the other side, it can do so because it initiates the outbound connection. But if the other side must open a connection to the offerer behind the NAT, the NAT rejects it—the offerer never initiated communication in that direction.

This RFC solves the problem by adopting COMEDIA (Connection-Oriented Media, defined in RFC 4145), a mechanism that lets both sides negotiate which one will open the TCP connection. An endpoint behind a NAT can say "I will open the connection," guaranteeing the connection passes through its NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: MSRP needs to open a connection. Normally, the person who starts the conversation opens it. But if you are behind a firewall that blocks incoming connections, you must be the one to open it or the firewall will reject the other person trying to reach you.

sections.title: COMEDIA and the a=setup Attribute
sections.content:
COMEDIA uses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes to signal connection negotiation. The key attribute is a=setup, which can have four values:

active: "I will open the TCP connection."
passive: "You open the TCP connection."
actpass: "I can do either; you decide."
holdconn: An older value that MSRP ignores.

An MSRP endpoint must include an explicit a=setup attribute in every SDP offer and answer. This tells the other side whether the endpoint supports COMEDIA or expects the traditional MSRP connection model.

The rules are: An endpoint offering the session MUST use actpass if it can provide a globally reachable IP address (no NAT, relayed through a proxy, or using STUN to detect the NAT address). It MUST use active if it cannot. It MUST NOT use passive in an offer. When answering, the endpoint MAY use active if the offer was actpass, or it SHOULD use passive if it knows it is not behind a NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: In the SDP handshake, each side announces whether it will open the connection (active), wants the other side to open it (passive), or is flexible (actpass). The endpoint behind the firewall can choose to open the connection to make sure it works.

sections.title: Address and Port in SDP
sections.content:
When an endpoint declares itself passive or actpass, the MSRP URI in the SDP a=path attribute MUST contain the actual IP address and port where the endpoint can receive a TCP connection. This is the listening address.

When an endpoint declares itself active, the port number in the MSRP URI should be 9, a placeholder indicating that the endpoint will connect to the other side, not listen on that port.

An MSRP endpoint can determine that it provides a globally reachable address in several ways: by detecting that it is not behind a NAT, by relaying MSRP connections through an MSRP relay or TURN server, or by using STUN signaling to discover the NAT's external address and verifying that the NAT has endpoint-independent mapping and filtering behavior. Some endpoints detect NAT by comparing SIP Via header addresses between what they sent and what the server echoed back, though this method does not work in all network topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: If you say you will listen for a connection, you tell the other side where to find you. If you say you will open the connection, you give a placeholder port number because you will connect outward, not listen.

sections.title: Opening the Connection and Sending the First Message
sections.content:
Once both sides agree on connection direction via the a=setup negotiation, the active endpoint opens the TCP connection and must immediately send an MSRP SEND request. The passive endpoint waits to receive the connection and infers the identity of the connecting side from the associated session description.

The Sieve URN parameter "addrbook" is used to identify address books. The mandatory one is urn:ietf:params:sieve:addrbook:default, referring to the user's default personal address book. Scripts can also reference :addrbook:personal, :addrbook:family, :addrbook:company, or implementation-defined variations.
sections.plainLanguage: The active side opens the connection and says hello first. The passive side accepts the connection and knows it came from the session it negotiated. Both sides then exchange messages normally.

sections.title: Transport Layer Security
sections.content:
When using Transport Layer Security (TLS) to encrypt MSRP messages, the active endpoint takes the role of TLS client, and the passive endpoint acts as TLS server. Endpoints can authenticate using self-signed certificates if they include the certificate fingerprint in the SDP.

Note that fingerprints are only exchanged in peer-to-peer communication. MSRP relays do not receive SDP payloads containing fingerprint attributes, so they cannot participate in fingerprint-based authentication.

TLS security is not affected by which endpoint is active or passive—RFC 4975 procedures remain unchanged. The level of authentication and encryption provided by TLS works the same way regardless of connection direction.
sections.plainLanguage: If you encrypt the messages with TLS, the side that opens the connection acts as the client, and the side that listens acts as the server. Both can prove who they are using certificate fingerprints.

sections.title: MSRP Relays and Relay Connections
sections.content:
An MSRP endpoint can relay its messages through an MSRP relay (a server that forwards messages between endpoints). When an endpoint is behind an MSRP relay, it MUST always initiate the TCP connection to the relay, regardless of the a=setup attribute negotiated with the remote endpoint. This ensures the endpoint can reach the relay.

However, the endpoint will only send an MSRP SEND request if the COMEDIA negotiation makes it active. This preserves the session semantics: the passive endpoint receives the connection from the relay and binds it to the correct message session.
sections.plainLanguage: When you go through a relay, you must connect to the relay so it can forward your messages. But whether you actually send messages depends on the COMEDIA negotiation with the other person.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility and Interoperability
sections.content:
An MSRP endpoint that supports COMEDIA (this RFC) can interoperate with endpoints that follow only the original RFC 4975 connection model. However, if a COMEDIA-supporting endpoint is behind a NAT, does not use an MSRP relay, and receives an SDP offer from an endpoint that does not support COMEDIA, NAT traversal fails. The only solutions then are to use ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) for TCP or rely on a Session Border Controller (SBC) to assist with NAT traversal.

The requirement to always include an explicit a=setup attribute helps: when an older endpoint receives it, it may not understand it, but it signals that the newer endpoint supports COMEDIA. The older endpoint can fall back to its traditional behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: New COMEDIA endpoints can talk to old endpoints if both are in the clear. But if a COMEDIA endpoint is behind a firewall and an old endpoint tries to connect, it will not work without a relay or a complex protocol like ICE.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
COMEDIA does not change the fundamental security model. The RFC 4975 requirement that the active party immediately sends an MSRP SEND request after establishing the connection still holds—this allows the passive party to bind the inbound connection to the correct message session.

With COMEDIA, either the offer sender or the offer receiver can become active, whereas traditionally only the offer sender could. This flexibility creates no new security weakness: the mechanism for identifying which endpoint owns the connection (via the SEND request) remains the same.

If TLS is used, the active endpoint becomes the TLS client. RFC 4975 procedures, which assume the offer sender is always active, do not break when the receiver becomes active instead. The security properties of TLS are not affected by which side opens the connection or takes the TLS client role.

Implementing this RFC is optional but strongly recommended for endpoints that may be deployed behind NATs, as it significantly improves the likelihood of successful connectivity without requiring relays.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting either side open the connection does not make things less secure. The first message still identifies who opened the connection, and encryption works the same way.
